text:

Thanks for your work on Solvespace. I have been using it for years. When I no longer had access to commercial CAD programs I tried all the open source stuff. My conclusions were:

* OpenSCAD -- cool idea, good for a few types of highly procedural parts, but most of the time I'd rather a parametric sketch-based interface over pure code.

* FreeCAD -- the most features of any open source CAD, but poor UI, tendency to crash, and the advanced features like loft kind of fall flat compared to commercial equivalents. You think you'll be able to model a part, but it becomes extremely frustrating if you actually need the advanced tools.

* SolveSpace -- pretty stable and reliable. Fast, compact, great sketching interface, good discoverable UI. You can predict what types of parts you can model with it and what types you can't. Doesn't try to do everything but is good at what it does.

You can tell which one is my favorite! N features done to a good level of polish and with somebody making sure it all "makes sense together" beats 10xN features all 80% done and haphazardly mashed together in different menus/workbenches, for any tools I want to rely on.

I am noodling around with a slopcoded CAD tool of my own these days, just out of curiosity to see how far Opus5.5/GPT6 can get doing it in F#. But for stuff I actually want to get done, SolveSpace remains my go-to, and I greatly admire its coherent design.

By all means, built a better system than git. In many respects, git sucks, and git upstream is not solving the major problems. But don’t lose the actual benefits of git!

BB(5) is also computable in the intuitive sense, because we proved its value: 47,176,870. In this sense BB(5) is just as computable as Graham's number. However there is likely a Busy Beaver number >5 that is intuitively uncomputable, such that there is no non-cheating algorithm which computes it. A cheating algorithm would be one that requires the knowledge of the result in advance to write the algorithm, in which case we wouldn't be able to come up with the algorithm in the first place, and we wouldn't know that the result is correct.

There is also a proof that the function BB(n) (with the free argument n) is uncomputable. However, this alone doesn't mean that e.g. BB(6) (a function with no free parameter) is or isn't intuitively computable. Though if you allow cheating, which is the case for the conventional academic definition of "computability", every particular constant function (that is, without a free parameter) would be considered "computable". Though that definition doesn't mean it is intuitively computable, because if you cheat, you aren't really computing something something, you are just reporting something without having computed it.

I contributed to this update because I think Sandstorm as a concept, improbably, is more important now than it was a decade ago. Some of the core ideas like aggressive sandboxing and a robust capabilities model were somewhat of a hindrance in the past: sandboxing made it difficult to port large existing OSS projects, and many apps didn’t implement capabilities. Now, agents can easily port OSS apps into Sandstorm, not to mention writing new bespoke applications directly within Sandstorm’s sandboxing. I think agents also make composing applications via capabilities very doable: in addition to each hosted app exposing a UI, it can expose an API in an interoperable shape that other Sandstorm apps can use.

Software is at an inflection point with agents where we have the opportunity to take back control of our apps and data from the large corporations and replace it with software we’ve written ourselves and run ourselves. I’m excited for how Sandstorm can enable this.

I'm currently building massive ETL pipelines that involve sifting through tons of heterogeneous types of data. That's the consumption side I'm talking about. Being able to extract semantic value from dissimilar sources and deductively and inductively draw conclusions about all sorts of things - the shape of data, behaviors, payloads, endpoint constraints, etc. - is enormously useful. Before LLMs, painstakingly analyzing every corner case was awfully time-consuming yet unavoidable. It's like using human labor vs. machines to collect, I dunno, cotton. Of course, machines can miss, but in general, humans would be still sloppier, just because humans do get tired, get hungry, get distracted, etc.

The Secure Enclave processor (SEP) is a separate processor that holds cryptographic material unique to the chip. That material is isolated from whatever compromise might happen on the main application processor; and there is no particular reason why you need more than one of them, even for multi-user. macOS has multiple users and uses the Secure Enclave just fine. For data encryption you'd have the SEP derive a different key for each user.

Secure Exclaves are special isolated processes that run on the same application processor as the regular OS. They're a very new OS feature and AFAIK Apple has barely talked about them until now.

Exclaves are isolated because Apple made a proprietary CPU extension called Guarded Exception Levels. It lets you separate an ARM exception level out into two privilege levels: guarded and unguarded. The guarded level can have different page permissions from the unguarded level, and switching between the two modes is extremely fast. Apple uses this to lock down iOS: its kernel, XNU, has it's entire virtual memory system hollowed out and replaced with a thing called the Secure Page Table Monitor (SPTM). XNU lives in EL2 (ARM hypervisor) but SPTM lives in GL2 (guarded hypervisor). In this configuration, SPTM is the only thing that can allocate memory, and it controls all memory allocations in the system. This is specifically why jailbreaks have become far harder to make[0]: you basically need to hack SPTM to get anything.

XNU, strangely enough, lives in both EL2 and EL1 (ARM kernel); but Apple also uses GL1 (guarded kernel) for a second, funnier OS called the Secure Kernel (SK). SK has its own exclusive resources and userland. Processes that run under SK cannot be tampered with or monitored by XNU because SPTM isolates them and their kernel from XNU. This is used for isolating any particularly security sensitive thing.

For example, code signing enforcement happens in an Exclave[1]. XNU can't run unsigned processes because it needs SPTM to bless the pages. But SPTM is supposed to be a very small attack surface; there is a long history of using memory safety bugs in the verification code to gain higher levels of privilege, so putting that code in GL2 would be bad. Instead, it gets put in an Exclave, where:

- A compromised XNU cannot tamper with the verifier, because SPTM won't give it write access to the pages.

- A compromised verifier doesn't compromise the whole system, because it's not part of SPTM/GL2.

- A compromised verifier can't interfere with other exclaves, because they're isolated by SK.

The only thing a compromised verifier can do is fail to reject an unsigned program, which would let you run specific unsigned code in EL0. You would not suddenly get kernel mode access from a verifier failure.

Anyway, what makes this relevant for HomeView is that all the microphone data processing can be isolated in an Exclave from the rest of the OS. So if the CIA wants to force your HomeView to listen to you, it needs to either compromise SPTM (very hard), or find a (non-memory-related) logic error in the listener exclave.

[0] This is also morally the same scheme as the Xbox 360 hypervisor that went decades without a softmod

[1] Morally speaking, it's an Exclave; it lives in GL0. But technically the code signing enforcement is in a different SPTM domain from the Secure Kernel, called the "Trusted Execution Monitor" (TXM). I would not be surprised if Apple migrates it over to an Exclave in the future.

Can you enforce it? Would you even know who to go after?

Traditionally cybercrimes have been prosecuted by the victim going to their local PD (or the FBI) with the IP address of the offender, and then law enforcement subpoenas the ISP associated with that IP address to figure out the customer associated with that account, and then they have a case for prosecution. It all works as long as cybercriminals are less numerous than law enforcement, fall in the same jurisdiction (or in jurisdictions that have reciprocal extradition treaties), and have a real identity that can be tied to their online activities.

Now, many law enforcement agencies are tied up prosecuting political opponents of their bosses. To the extent that they have bandwidth to investigate and prosecute ordinary crimes, they're going to prioritize the ones that target a.) the government that backs them (of which there are many - you see another headline about the government being hacked every week or so on HN) b.) major corporations that have sophisticated IT systems that can aid prosecution or c.) headlines that will get their boss a PR boost and themselves a promotion. Your personal website does not register among those priorities. You probably can't even prove damages from the intrusion itself. The perpetrator might be a Russian bot that the U.S. doesn't have jurisdiction over, or a Canadian teen that the U.S. previously might've been able to prosecute with reciprocal judicial treaties but now has no leverage over because we've blown up our relationship with Canada. It may be legally a crime, but economically it's not worth prosecution.

Traditionally security researchers had to be very careful because they were doing everything above-board, with their real identity attached to their actions, and they made a very attractive (and PR-worthy) target. Somebody who's port-scanning from Russia through a VPN or residential proxy network is a.) anonymous b.) untraceable c.) out of U.S. jurisdiction and d.) not a headline-worthy target anyway.

A couple years ago I predicted here that a lot of things will break as the U.S. transitions from a high-trust to a low-trust society. This is one of them. Much of our justice system works well when criminals are rare and utterly falls apart when they're ubiquitous.

>what's the meaning of '+' there?

Mathematicians often reuse the same notation for different things where it's clear (for the mathematicians) what the implied meaning is. That means however that non-mathematicians can get confused.

The plus here is the operation that we call "the sum of complex numbers", where the numbers are a and bi. We can work towards this by first defining complex numbers as a tuple of two real numbers with particular sum and multiplication laws for these tuples. So (a, b) + (c, d) = (a + b, c + d) where the left side plus is for complex numbers and the right side plus is for real numbers. Similarly for multiplication, (a, b) * (c, d) = (ac - bd, bc + ad).

We associate (1,0) with the real number 1, and similarly for tuples of the form (a,0). The association is what allows us to see the real numbers as a subset of the complex numbers rather than being some unrelated set. It makes sense because the set of tuples of the form (a,0) with the multiplication laws of complex numbers behaves the same way as the real numbers and is in 1:1 correspondence with them. This association is used every time we write (a,0) as a(1,0) or just "a". We also write (0,b) as b(0,1) since (b,0)*(0,1) = (0,b), from the multiplication law. A general tuple (a, b) then can be written as (a,0) + (0,b) or, as what we've said is the same thing, a + b(0,1). Now we have simplified notation for all of these things except (0,1). It follows from the multiplication law that (0,1)*(0,1) = -(1,0) = -1. The complex number whose square is -1 is denoted as i. All these simplifications allow you to write (a,b) as a + bi.

> More fundamentally what's addition and multiplication? Is there a continuity between them, like an operator that represents both addition and multiplication meeting them half-way?

I'm not personally aware of any concept of continuity between these operations. In abstract algebra, operations are fundamental to an algebraic structure. The field of real numbers or the field of complex numbers are algebraic structures defined by their elements, the binary operation called addition, the binary operation called multiplication, and the laws that these operations satisfy. For example, both are commutative and associative, but the distribution law shows that they're different: a*(b+c) = a*b + a*c, but not a+b*c = (a+b)*(a+c). Also, a+0 = a, but a*1 = a, so the operations have different special elements that "fix" the other element when an operation is applied. The idea of complex numbers and the more general idea of field extensions, which describes the process of obtaining complex numbers from reals, came from the study of polynomials. Polynomials can only have terms of integer degree. They satisfy many nice properties and quite rich mathematical structures arise from them which would not be possible with general non-integer degrees. Second degree polynomials with real coefficients, like x^2 + 1, are the lowest-degree polynomials such that they may not have real roots, and x^2 + 1 is the simplest example, but any other polynomial can be used to produce the complex numbers as well, if has a factor like x^2 + a. This is where the 2 comes from. It's not significant from a real line perspective (2 is just a number among the infinite reals) but it's significant from an algebraic one.

title: Show HN: Treesum – Replace MS Excel/Project with a Code Editor
text:
# Intro

The goal of this software is to make it easy to get the plan that's in your head onto the page. Start with the outline then add details. Then more details. Then numbers: costs, time, quantities. Then organize and categorize with #tags. All the sums, graphs and pivot table functionality happens automatically in the Calcs, Timeline, Stats views. And everything looks nice without you having to format it.

Currently, it's all local, saved in your browser. Save your plan permanently by downloading the '.tsum' file. Open (upload) the '.tsum' to start working again. Everything happens in the browser. The files are stored where ever you like. The '.tsum' file is just text - human and AI readable. Use it to plan anything. We hope it works like your brain does - by organizing things in trees.

# Story

This software is entirely vibe-coded. It had to be - none of my developer friends would help me out. The front end JS on this app is too complex for a part time developer like myself. I've had this idea for a while and was only able to bring it to life because of AI. It may not gain traction, but at least I can put it out there, use it myself, or stop thinking about it altogether. It's amazing to see it and actually use it - to know if my idea was good or not, at least for me. And I'm actually happy with it and have been using it. If you have thoughts about the idea, feel free to let me know. I'm open to suggestions for improvement.

# Disclaimer

This tool is mainly intended to help with project planning. But it can be used for any data that looks more like a tree than a table. Creating a quote or estimate for one-off projects is my favorite use case. The varying structure of costs across lumber, electrical, concrete and labor fits well.

Obviously, it doesn't replace all the many things Excel can do. It tries to improve on MS Project by making it easier to get your schedule on the page by coding into an editor instead of poking at menus in a GUI. It is still a proof of concept at this point, not a bullet-proof software package. If there's interest, it will be developed further. For now, it's good enough for me.

# Roadmap

I want this software to be the Excalidraw of Excel: free, simple, browser-based and fun to use. There are great things that Excalidraw does that would require servers and more costs. These features could be turned into a paid product if there is interest. So, if you're interested, please let me know: treesum.app (at) gmail.com.

# Thanks HN

This project would not have been possible with out AI. But also not without HN. Reading HN nearly every work day really shapes how to think about software and presenting it to people - especially for someone who is not a full-time developer. It's a great community and I've happily been a member since (at least) 2013.

Terminological nitpick, but soundness is a property of an entire type system not of an individual program. A type system is sound if it only accepts valid programs. A program is valid if it never exhibits undefined behavior.
